evidence.currentDescription: Ordinary worship, prayer, and moral imitation allegedly produce practical fruits across theological models, so speculative system-building should not displace accessible religious participation despite unresolved doctrine.
evidence.lockedProposition: Ordinary worship, prayer, and moral imitation bear fruits across theological schemes, so speculative efforts to perfect the system should not displace religious practice.

evidence.assessmentRationale: Strongest feature: The closing move returns clearly to the practical motion and identifies concrete activities—worship, prayer, and moral imitation—that can be undertaken without complete metaphysical certainty. Principal limitation: The promised fruits remain unspecified and comparatively unevidenced, while calling doctrinal tensions distractions bypasses the objection that different religions prescribe incompatible relationships with ultimate reality. Live burden: The affirmative must establish what benefits arise, why they indicate truth or obligation, and whether comparable secular or alternative practices deliver them with fewer risks of conceptual error.
